idea_text:
Most end-to-end driving policies assume that sensing, inference, and control occur as one synchronized operation. Real vehicles instead receive camera, LiDAR, localization, and route updates at different times, while inference occasionally misses deadlines. The obvious response is to augment training with random delays. That still asks a learned model to discover timing robustness empirically and permits a late packet to rewrite an action that the vehicle has already begun executing.

The proposed research direction is to make **physical commitment, rather than inference steps or sensor frames, the unit of planning**. The policy continuously emits refinements to one timestamped trajectory. At every update, a deterministic control layer computes the interval of motion that is already irreversible, given actuator delay, steering and acceleration-rate limits, and the commands currently queued on the vehicle. The new plan must exactly preserve that committed prefix. It may modify only the suffix that remains physically reachable from the state at the end of the prefix.

This constraint can be constructed rather than learned. Let the previous plan be \(u_{0:H}\), and let \(k\) be the earliest command index that can still be changed before execution. Propagate the vehicle’s bounded state uncertainty through \(u_{0:k-1}\), producing a set of possible states at \(k\). A scene-conditioned generative model may propose any collection of suffixes, but each proposal is accepted only if it starts from every state in that set, respects vehicle dynamics, and avoids conservative obstacle-occupancy sets. A short robust optimization then selects the feasible suffix minimizing deviation from the proposal and driving cost. If multiple sensor packets arrive during computation, they update obstacle sets and candidate suffixes but cannot alter the committed prefix. If computation stops at any instant, the latest certified plan remains executable.

The key invariant is:

> Two executions receiving the same timestamped sensor packets but experiencing different inference runtimes produce identical controls over every interval that had become physically committed before their information histories diverged.

This follows directly from prefix preservation, rather than from model generalization. It removes a dangerous race condition in which faster or differently scheduled inference changes an action too late for the vehicle to realize the corresponding trajectory. It also permits computation to be genuinely anytime: additional denoising, search, or perception improves only future, still-revisable motion.

Robust safety requires a terminal fallback condition. Every accepted suffix must end in a set from which a fixed emergency controller can remain collision-free under stated bounds on localization error, actuator response, and other agents’ short-horizon motion. If no proposed suffix satisfies this condition, the optimizer appends the fallback maneuver rather than extrapolating a learned plan. The safety claim is deliberately limited to environments satisfying those explicit bounds; unpredictable agents outside them trigger a declared loss of guarantee rather than a silent claim of robustness.

The step most likely to degenerate is conservative occupancy prediction: sufficiently broad uncertainty could reject every normal driving trajectory. It does not make the mechanism undefined because the maintained fallback trajectory supplies a feasible candidate whenever the system remains inside its certified operating envelope. Frequent fallback activation is then a measurable coverage failure of the uncertainty model or sensor setup, not something hidden by planner averages.

Evaluation would replay identical closed-loop scenarios under adversarially varied packet delays, dropped modalities, and inference preemption. Besides collisions and progress, the central metric would be **post-commitment revision**: the physical discrepancy between controls already implied by an accepted plan and controls later requested for the same interval. The proposed construction makes this quantity zero up to numerical tolerance, while ordinary delay-augmented policies have no reason to satisfy it. This attacks latency as a consistency problem at the boundary between computation and physics, rather than as another distribution shift for imitation learning.

final_idea_core.core_claim: Instead of training models to implicitly handle delays, physical commitment is made the fundamental unit of planning, allowing only the physically reachable future trajectory to be revised by new information.
final_idea_core.mechanism: The system continuously refines a timestamped trajectory, ensuring that all new plans strictly preserve the prefix of motion that has already become physically irreversible due to actuator limits and queued commands.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Current end-to-end driving policies struggle with asynchronous sensor inputs and inference delays, leading to unsafe or inconsistent vehicle actions.
final_idea_core.source_gap: A deterministic control layer can accurately and robustly compute the exact interval of physically committed motion at any given time.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: The system will exhibit zero post-commitment revision (physical discrepancy between planned and executed controls for already committed intervals), ensuring consistent and safer vehicle behavior despite varying inference runtimes and sensor delays.

idea_text:
Current end-to-end planners represent uncertainty as a set or distribution of complete trajectories. This is the wrong object when different actions become appropriate only after future evidence arrives—for example, entering an occluded intersection if it clears versus yielding if a pedestrian appears. Sampling more trajectories does not solve this: the controller must select one before observing which world is real, so trajectory diversity can create premature commitment rather than robustness.

The proposed idea is to predict a **contingent driving plan: a shared initial action followed by branches triggered by future observations**. This imports the non-anticipativity principle from stochastic optimization: two possible worlds must receive identical actions for as long as the vehicle cannot distinguish them from its observations.

At each replanning step, a scene model produces a finite set of hypotheses about currently unresolved variables, such as an occluded agent’s presence and velocity. Each hypothesis includes predicted future sensor evidence, not merely a future scene trajectory. A planner then constructs a tree whose nodes contain short control segments and whose edges are tests on observable quantities—for example, occupancy appearing in a specified sensor region. Hypotheses with indistinguishable predicted observation histories are forced to share the same control prefix. They may receive different controls only after their predicted observations separate by more than a calibrated sensor-error bound. Thus, a branch cannot depend on hidden state unavailable to the vehicle.

Training uses logged sequences with temporary masking to recreate earlier information states. The demonstrated continuation supervises the realized branch, while alternative hypotheses are supplied by a calibrated multi-object perception model and constrained by map geometry, vehicle dynamics, and sensor visibility. Counterfactual branches need not imitate nonexistent demonstrations: they are optimized with ordinary dynamics-based costs and collision constraints. Learning is used to rank comfortable feasible trees and approximate their construction, but a runtime projection enforces dynamics, branch predicates, and non-anticipativity exactly. The executed action is always the common root segment; after new sensor data arrives, inconsistent branches are removed and the tree is rebuilt.

The most obvious competent alternative is to generate diverse trajectories, attach probabilities, and choose a conservative or high-scoring sample. That still chooses among mutually exclusive futures at the present time. The conceptual change here is that uncertainty changes **when a decision is permitted**, not just which trajectory receives the highest score.

The central property holds by construction. Let two hypotheses have observation histories whose distance remains within the sensor uncertainty set through time \(t\). The planner places them in the same information partition and imposes equality of their controls through \(t\). Consequently, the vehicle cannot act differently because of information it has not yet obtained. Calibration errors can still omit the true hypothesis, so evaluation must separately measure hypothesis coverage; conformal calibration on held-out sequences can set the uncertainty sets to a target empirical coverage level without claiming absolute real-world guarantees.

The step most likely to degenerate is the shared-prefix constraint: under severe ambiguity, no moving action may be safe for every retained hypothesis. This does not produce an arbitrary average trajectory. The planner includes a dynamically verified minimum-risk stop or controlled-creep maneuver as a mandatory fallback and explicitly reports the tree as robustly infeasible if even that maneuver violates the safety envelope. Controlled creeping is allowed only when it improves future visibility while remaining safe under all current hypotheses. The resulting research question is whether information-consistent contingent plans reduce occlusion and intersection failures compared with equally accurate single-trajectory, multimodal, and uncertainty-penalized planners—especially when the correct behavior depends on evidence that arrives only after planning begins.

final_idea_core.core_claim: It explicitly enforces the non-anticipativity principle by making action branches conditional on *future observable evidence* rather than hidden state, forcing hypotheses with identical predicted observations to share control prefixes.
final_idea_core.mechanism: The system predicts a contingent driving plan, represented as a tree of shared initial actions followed by branches triggered by future observations, enforcing identical actions for indistinguishable observation histories.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Current end-to-end autonomous driving planners prematurely commit to a single future trajectory despite uncertainty, leading to brittleness in situations requiring future observation-contingent actions.
final_idea_core.source_gap: Future sensor evidence and the corresponding observation-history separability can be reliably predicted and used to define decision branching points, rather than just future scene trajectories.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: Contingent plans will reduce occlusion and intersection failures by enabling context-appropriate actions based on newly acquired sensor data, outperforming single-trajectory, multimodal, and uncertainty-penalized planners, especially where evidence arrive…

idea_text:
Most driving policies represent uncertainty as a set of open-loop trajectories sampled independently at every control cycle. This confuses two different phenomena: uncertainty that should persist until new evidence arrives, and variation caused merely by resampling. The result is “mode flicker”: a vehicle alternates between braking, proceeding, and changing lanes even though its observations have barely changed. Receding-horizon smoothing treats the symptom, while the obvious competent approach—adding temporal losses or warm-starting the next diffusion sample—cannot distinguish justified plan changes from arbitrary ones.

The proposed idea is to learn a sequence of conditional plan distributions that must satisfy the same information-consistency law as Bayesian beliefs. Let \(H_t\) denote all observations available by time \(t\), and let \(M\) be a future maneuver event defined directly from the executed trajectory, such as “enter the intersection before stopping,” “pass ahead of the approaching vehicle,” or, more generally, membership in a fixed measurable partition of trajectory space. A coherent policy must satisfy

\[
P(M\mid H_t)
=
\mathbb{E}\!\left[P(M\mid H_{t+1})\mid H_t\right].
\]

Thus the probability assigned now must equal the average probability assigned after one more observation. New evidence may move probability between modes, but in expectation the policy cannot manufacture or erase confidence merely because another control cycle elapsed.

Training uses logged sequences rather than isolated frames. A trajectory-density model predicts the distribution of future ego motion from every prefix \(H_t\). A separate observation-transition model estimates the distribution of the next sensor representation given \(H_t\); it is used only to evaluate the expectation above. The policy is trained both by proper likelihood scoring on demonstrated futures and by violations of the tower-consistency equation across many trajectory events. Events are not learned semantic labels: they are generated deterministically from trajectories using occupancy regions, ordering relations with other actors, stopping intervals, and multiscale action-space partitions. Refining these partitions makes consistency increasingly constrain the full trajectory distribution rather than a small hand-selected set of maneuvers.

At deployment, the policy does not independently resample a mode each cycle. It maintains one persistent random quantile and transports it through successive conditional distributions. Concretely, candidate trajectories are sorted by a deterministic hierarchical partition of action space; the previous quantile identifies a probability mass element, and the updated observation moves that same mass element through the newly predicted distribution. If evidence changes mode probabilities enough that the element crosses a boundary, the plan switches; otherwise its high-level decision persists. Low-level controls are still recomputed from the latest observation, so persistence does not imply blindly executing an obsolete open-loop trajectory.

The key construction is that plan changes are coupled to information changes rather than elapsed denoising or replanning steps. If observations reveal that an occluded pedestrian is entering the road, posterior mass shifts toward stopping and the persistent quantile switches accordingly. If observations are unchanged, the coupling preserves the selected mode even though each cycle produces a newly conditioned trajectory. This addresses a failure that greater trajectory diversity alone cannot solve: a collection of plausible plans is not yet a coherent sequential policy.

The step most likely to degenerate is the consistency constraint becoming vacuous because the next-observation model simply imitates the policy’s probabilities. To prevent this, that model is trained independently by a proper predictive objective on actual next observations, receives no policy outputs, and is frozen when computing consistency. Its adequacy is directly testable by held-out next-observation likelihood and calibration. Moreover, the identity is evaluated both through this model and through empirical successor prefixes in logged data; disagreement exposes transition-model bias rather than silently validating the policy.

The central claim is deliberately narrower than collision avoidance: the method guarantees distributional temporal coherence relative to the learned observation process, not safety or perfect forecasting. Experiments should therefore isolate unjustified mode switching, probability calibration before and after informative events, reaction delay when genuine evidence appears, closed-loop comfort, and collision rates under occlusion and ambiguous right-of-way. The decisive comparison is against independent resampling, warm starts, and trajectory-smoothing losses at matched one-step imitation accuracy.

final_idea_core.core_claim: Instead of resampling, the policy maintains a persistent random quantile that is transported through successive conditional distributions, causing plan changes only when new evidence shifts probability mass across predefined maneuver boundaries.
final_idea_core.mechanism: The policy learns a sequence of conditional plan distributions that satisfy a Bayesian information-consistency law, ensuring that current probability assignments align with the expected future assignments after one more observation.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Autonomous driving policies suffer from "mode flicker," where vehicles repeatedly switch between maneuvers due to independent trajectory resampling at each control cycle, rather than in response to new evidence.
final_idea_core.source_gap: The observation-transition model, used to evaluate the consistency constraint, accurately predicts future observations and is not degenerate or biased to imitate policy probabilities.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: The driving policy will exhibit significantly reduced unjustified mode switching, improved probability calibration, and faster reaction to genuine evidence, while maintaining comparable one-step imitation accuracy to baseline methods.

idea_text:
Current end-to-end planners represent uncertainty as several complete ego trajectories. This is conceptually wrong for many driving ambiguities: whether to proceed often depends on information that will arrive later, such as an occluded pedestrian becoming visible or another vehicle beginning to yield. A set of open-loop trajectories allows the planner to commit immediately to a branch whose justification is not yet observable.

The proposed research direction is to predict **sensor-contingent plan trees rather than trajectory distributions**. Each tree has a shared initial control sequence followed by branches guarded by future, directly measurable conditions—for example, “the tracked vehicle’s conservative time-to-intersection interval is now above four seconds.” Until a guard is resolved, every branch must prescribe the same action. Thus diversity represents future contingency, not arbitrary present-time choice.

Training data would be produced from controlled simulator forks. Starting from one identical hidden world state, randomize only an unresolved variable such as an occluded actor’s motion, traffic-light transition, or another driver’s yielding decision. Run a privileged expert in every fork and record both expert controls and the onboard sensor histories. The supervision target is obtained by merging these rollouts subject to a non-anticipativity constraint: two forks must share controls for as long as their sensor histories remain indistinguishable within specified perception-error bounds. They may branch only at the first time their observable uncertainty sets become disjoint. Optimization finds the lowest-cost shared prefix that remains collision-free in every still-indistinguishable fork, followed by fork-specific continuations. The learned model maps the current sensor history and route to this tree; during deployment, a small deterministic executor follows the shared prefix and selects a branch only when its guard is certified from the current uncertainty-bounded tracks.

The construction supplies the central invariant: **worlds that cannot yet be distinguished from onboard information receive identical actions**. This prevents information leakage from simulator state during training and prevents a learned planner from acting as though it already knows an actor’s future intent. Safety of the prefix can additionally be checked by propagating reachable occupancy sets for every unresolved fork; learning proposes the tree, but the branch timing and prefix validity are mechanically verified.

The obvious competent solution is to sample more trajectories, improve their scores, and replan frequently. That still ranks mutually exclusive futures before the evidence separating them exists. The discontinuous causal lever here is to change the output from a distribution over actions into a policy over future observations, explicitly enforcing when a decision is legally allowed to depend on information.

The most likely degeneracy is that conservative perception bounds never separate, so no branch can fire. This does not yield an arbitrary or all-zero signal: the executor continues the robust shared prefix, usually controlled slowing, and transitions to a certified minimum-risk stop if no common safe continuation exists. Such states are labeled as “no jointly safe prefix” during tree construction rather than being forced into a misleading branch. Evaluation should separately measure collision rate, unnecessary braking, branch decisions made before their evidence became observable, and performance under altered actor-intent frequencies. The central hypothesis is that this representation will improve closed-loop behavior specifically in occlusion and interaction scenarios where trajectory diversity currently conflates “choices available now” with “actions that become appropriate only after learning something later.”

final_idea_core.core_claim: It enforces that worlds indistinguishable from onboard information receive identical actions, preventing premature commitment and ensuring decisions depend only on observed evidence.
final_idea_core.mechanism: The method predicts sensor-contingent plan trees, where initial actions are shared across indistinguishable futures and branches are guarded by directly measurable, future sensor conditions.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Current end-to-end planners incorrectly represent driving ambiguities by committing to actions based on unobservable future information, leading to unsafe or inefficient decisions.
final_idea_core.source_gap: Perception bounds will eventually separate sufficiently to allow safe branching in ambiguous scenarios.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: The approach will improve closed-loop driving behavior, specifically in occlusion and interaction scenarios, by reducing collisions and unnecessary braking compared to trajectory-distribution planners.

idea_text:
The central problem is not that driving policies fail to represent enough trajectory modes; it is that they are forced to commit to a mode before observations justify that commitment. At an occluded intersection, for example, “go” and “yield” are not merely two actions to sample and rank. They are branches associated with different hidden worlds. A planner should first choose an action that keeps safe continuations available in both worlds, then commit after new evidence arrives.

The obvious competent approach is to generate diverse trajectories and select the highest-scoring or safest one. That still makes an open-loop commitment under the current belief. Instead, the proposed method learns **contingent plans whose initial segment is chosen by backward reachability, not by trajectory probability**.

At each control cycle, perception produces a bounded set of scene hypotheses: possible occupancies and motions of visible and occluded agents over a short horizon. These hypotheses can come from any probabilistic predictor, but they are converted into sets using held-out calibration so that their empirical miss rate is explicit. For each hypothesis, a dynamics-based reachability calculation determines the ego states from which at least one collision-free, dynamically feasible continuation remains possible. The vehicle then selects a short control prefix that keeps its resulting state inside the intersection of these continuation sets. Thus, the prefix need not resemble the average of demonstrated actions or any complete sampled trajectory. It may creep forward to improve visibility, delay a lane change, or reduce speed just enough to preserve both stopping and proceeding as future options.

After executing only that prefix, the planner incorporates the next observation, removes hypotheses contradicted by sensor evidence, recomputes the reachable sets, and repeats. Demonstrations are used only to rank controls within the option-preserving set—for comfort, progress, and human driving style—not to define safety or determine which uncertainty branch is true. This cleanly separates imitation from the logically prior question of whether an action destroys all safe responses to a still-plausible world.

The key invariant is constructive: if the true scene evolution belongs to the calibrated hypothesis set, the ego dynamics lie within their bounded uncertainty, and the current state lies in the computed intersection, then every executed prefix leaves at least one feasible safe continuation under every still-plausible hypothesis. This follows directly from the definition of the backward-reachable sets rather than from an emergent learned behavior. A robust invariant terminal set—such as remaining stopped before the conflict region—is included so finite-horizon calculations do not falsely certify actions whose collision occurs just beyond the horizon.

The step most likely to degenerate is intersection of the continuation sets: in dense traffic it may be empty. The method therefore does not silently average incompatible branches. It first shortens the committed prefix, since fewer irreversible actions can restore a nonempty intersection. If none exists, it switches to a separately verified minimum-risk controller selected against the full hypothesis set, including rear traffic; it reports the state as uncertifiable rather than claiming safety. If no collision-free action physically exists, the method makes no impossible guarantee, but minimizes worst-case impact subject to vehicle limits.

A decisive evaluation would construct matched scenarios in which the current sensor frame is identical but later observations reveal different hidden worlds. Compare against single-trajectory regression, multimodal sampling, and risk-based trajectory ranking. The primary measurements should be premature commitment rate, probability of retaining a safe continuation after each executed prefix, collision rate conditional on hypothesis-set coverage, and progress once ambiguity resolves. The research claim is not that uncertainty prediction becomes perfect, but that conditional on the represented uncertainty, the policy’s treatment of ambiguity is correct by construction: it preserves options until evidence supports commitment.

final_idea_core.core_claim: The method chooses control prefixes to keep the ego state within the intersection of reachable sets from multiple scene hypotheses, explicitly delaying commitment until new observations reduce ambiguity.
final_idea_core.mechanism: It learns contingent plans by selecting an initial control prefix using backward reachability from all plausible future world hypotheses, ensuring safe continuations remain available across all present uncertainties.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Autonomous driving policies prematurely commit to a single trajectory mode before sufficient observational evidence, leading to unsafe or suboptimal decisions in ambiguous scenarios like occluded intersections.
final_idea_core.source_gap: The true scene evolution and ego dynamics consistently remain within the calibrated set of hypotheses and their bounded uncertainties, allowing reachability calculations to reliably preserve future options.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: It will significantly reduce premature commitment rates and increase the probability of retaining a safe continuation throughout ambiguous situations, conditional on the uncertainty representation's coverage.

idea_text:
Current generative driving policies represent uncertainty by producing several complete trajectories and selecting one immediately. This is the wrong object under partial observability: at an occluded intersection, “go” and “yield” may both be reasonable, but the vehicle should not commit before the hidden car becomes observable. The most obvious competent remedy is better uncertainty scoring or more diverse trajectory samples. Instead, the proposed planner outputs a **contingent plan whose branches are tied to future observations**, and enforces that actions cannot differ before the evidence distinguishing those branches becomes available.

At each control cycle, a calibrated scene model constructs a finite set of possible world evolutions consistent with sensor history—for example, an empty occluded lane, or vehicles emerging from each physically reachable hidden position. Coverage is more important than probability: rare but feasible hypotheses remain represented. Each hypothesis predicts both obstacle motion and the observations the ego vehicle would receive under candidate ego actions, including how creeping changes visibility.

The planner then jointly optimizes a tree of ego trajectories. Two hypotheses must share exactly the same controls while their predicted observation histories are indistinguishable within sensor resolution. Their controls may branch only after an observation separates them. Thus, a plan cannot “know” that an unseen vehicle exists merely because that hypothesis was sampled. Collision constraints are imposed separately on every represented hypothesis, while progress and imitation costs choose among safe trees. Receding-horizon execution applies only the common first control, receives the next observation, removes inconsistent hypotheses, and follows or recomputes the corresponding branch. A learned network may amortize tree proposal, but a deterministic online checker enforces observation-based branch timing and hypothesis-wise collision constraints; failed proposals fall back to a robust stop or bounded creep action.

The key guarantee is a non-anticipativity invariant: if two possible worlds have produced the same available observations, the planner issues the same action in both. Conditional on the hypothesis set containing the true evolution and the dynamics bounds being valid, the executed prefix satisfies the collision constraints for the true world. This is a construction-level guarantee, not an expectation that a diffusion model will learn appropriate caution. Statistical calibration can set hypothesis-set coverage on held-out sequences, while deliberately withheld occluded-agent scenarios test failures outside that coverage.

The step most likely to degenerate is distinguishability: two hypotheses may remain observationally identical for the entire horizon. That does not produce an empty signal or arbitrary averaging. The invariant simply forbids branching, forcing a common action safe in both worlds—usually stopping, or creeping only if every hypothesis remains collision-free. Conversely, overly broad hypothesis sets may cause excessive caution; this is addressed without deleting low-probability hazards by planning information-gathering motions that expose occluded space and by measuring the progress–coverage tradeoff explicitly.

Evaluation should compare against single-trajectory regression, diverse trajectory generation, and risk-sensitive planning on matched perception. The decisive tests are counterfactual pairs with identical initial observations but different hidden traffic, measuring premature commitment, collision rate, time to acquire distinguishing evidence, and progress after evidence arrives. The research claim is not merely improved multimodal prediction: driving uncertainty should be represented as **when future actions are allowed to diverge based on future evidence**, rather than as several incompatible open-loop trajectories chosen from current information.

idea_text:
Most driving models treat uncertainty as a need to generate several complete trajectories and then select one. The more fundamental problem is that many traffic modes should not be resolved at planning time at all. At an occluded intersection, for example, “proceed” and “yield” may remain observationally indistinguishable, while both permit the same short, low-speed approach. Prematurely selecting either full trajectory creates avoidable collisions or unnecessary stops.

The proposed policy would therefore predict neither a single trajectory nor a distribution over complete trajectories. It would compute the longest action prefix that remains recoverably safe under every scene evolution consistent with the sensor history, and postpone mode selection until new observations distinguish the possibilities.

A learned sensor model first produces bounds—not probabilities—on currently occupied space, possible hidden-agent locations, and their admissible velocities. These bounds are propagated forward using physical acceleration and road-connectivity limits. Coverage calibration on held-out drives enlarges the bounds so that, at a chosen error rate, the true scene evolution lies within them. Route intent and imitation data provide only a cost over candidate ego motions; they never define safety.

Planning then builds candidate ego trajectories and evaluates their braking and steering-recovery envelopes against every admissible environment evolution. Two candidate trajectories can share an executable prefix even if their later behaviors differ, such as continuing through an intersection versus stopping before the conflict region. The vehicle executes the longest shared prefix for which each possible continuation still has at least one collision-free recovery. It replans as observations arrive. If uncertainty cannot yet be resolved, it may creep forward only when the complete stopping envelope during that creep lies inside currently certified free space. Thus creeping can improve visibility without assuming that unseen space is empty. If even that condition fails, stopping is the correct output.

The key invariant is recursive recoverability: after every executed prefix, for every world still consistent with the observations, at least one safe continuation remains. This can be checked with conservative reachable-set intersections rather than learned by imitation. Consequently, the claimed safety effect does not depend on whether a trajectory generator assigns good probabilities to rare modes. Conditional on the calibrated scene bounds and stated dynamics limits containing reality, the vehicle cannot enter a state from which all admissible worlds require incompatible emergency responses.

The most likely degeneration is excessive conservatism: uncertainty bounds could make every useful prefix empty, reducing the policy to permanent stopping. The mechanism addresses—but does not conceal—this failure in two ways. First, hidden-agent reachability is constrained by physically traversable road space and bounded dynamics, rather than allowing arbitrary occupancy everywhere. Second, visibility-improving motion is admitted whenever its stopping envelope remains in observed free space. An explicit diagnostic reports the fraction of time progress is blocked separately by perception bounds, dynamics bounds, and genuinely incompatible futures. If physically constrained bounds still imply no safe creep, no planner can soundly infer permission to proceed from the available sensors; additional sensing or infrastructure is required rather than a more confident learned policy.

The central experiment would compare this delayed-commitment policy with single-trajectory and multimodal planners in closed-loop scenarios containing controlled occlusions, rare agent behavior, localization error, and sensor latency. Beyond collision and route completion, evaluation would measure premature commitment rate, time spent conservatively blocked, calibration violations, and whether each executed prefix retained a verified recovery. The conceptual departure is to preserve ambiguity through action execution, rather than representing ambiguity more expressively and then forcing an immediate choice.

final_idea_core.mechanism: The policy computes and executes the longest action prefix that remains recoverably safe under every scene evolution consistent with sensor history, postponing mode selection.
final_idea_core.problem_targeted: Most driving models prematurely resolve inherent traffic mode ambiguities at planning time, leading to avoidable collisions or unnecessary stops.
final_idea_core.source_gap: The calibrated sensor model's bounds on occupied space, hidden agent locations, and velocities reliably contain the true scene evolution at a chosen error rate.
final_idea_core.expected_effect: The policy will reduce avoidable collisions and unnecessary stops in scenarios with occlusions and rare behaviors, while preventing the vehicle from entering states requiring incompatible emergency responses.

The central problem is not that driving demonstrations contain multiple valid trajectories; it is that identical sensor histories can correspond to different hidden worlds requiring incompatible actions. A pedestrian may or may not be behind an occluding van. Any policy that predicts a distribution over demonstrated trajectories can assign probabilities to these possibilities, but probability does not make an unsafe action safe. The most obvious approach is therefore to improve uncertainty prediction and sample more diverse plans. The proposed discontinuous move is instead to treat occlusion as an information constraint and permit only actions that remain safe in every physically possible hidden world consistent with what the vehicle has observed.

At each control cycle, the system constructs a set of scene completions rather than a single reconstructed scene. Visible free space and observed agents constrain all completions identically. Occluded road regions are populated adversarially with agents whose positions, sizes, and velocities satisfy map geometry, vehicle dynamics, visibility history, and conservative behavioral bounds. This does not require knowing the actual hidden scene: the set is computed from sensor-visible evidence and geometric occlusion. Temporal observations shrink it—for example, an unseen pedestrian cannot occupy a location that would have required crossing previously visible free space.

For each candidate short action sequence, a verified dynamics model propagates the ego vehicle and all admissible hidden agents over a braking horizon. The planner rejects the sequence if any completion can produce collision or violation of a stopping-distance constraint. It then selects the highest-preference sequence among the survivors, where preference can be learned from demonstrations or specified by progress and comfort costs. Thus learning chooses among already-safe actions; it is not responsible for discovering safety from data. Replanning repeatedly allows the vehicle to proceed once motion reveals enough of the occluded region.

The key training contribution is to make observational aliasing explicit. In simulation, generate families of worlds with exactly the same rendered sensor history up to the decision time but different hidden occupants. Compute the robustly admissible action set jointly over each family and train the policy to place support only inside that set. These paired worlds prevent the model from exploiting simulator-specific pixels or hidden labels: before reveal time, they are deliberately indistinguishable at the policy input. After reveal, their policies may diverge. Real logs can be used for preference learning without needing annotations of hypothetical hidden agents.

The construction gives a clear conditional guarantee. If the completion set contains the real hidden world, agent-motion bounds hold, and the vehicle tracks the selected sequence within stated error bounds, every accepted sequence is collision-free over the verified horizon. Sensor and control uncertainty are incorporated by enlarging visible-object states and ego reachable tubes rather than asking a learned confidence score to be calibrated.

The step most likely to degenerate is intersection of the safe action sets: under very conservative hidden-agent assumptions, no progress-making action may survive. This is not silently resolved by averaging incompatible plans. The system distinguishes “no progress action” from “no safe action.” It always includes a dynamically verified maximum-braking maneuver, provided the current state is still within a controlled-invariant stopping set; the planner is required to maintain membership in that set at every cycle. If even braking cannot satisfy the horizon constraint, the state was already unrecoverable and the guarantee correctly reports failure rather than fabricating a safe plan. Conservatism is reduced only through defensible constraints—visibility history, physical reachability, road topology, and newly revealed space—not by assigning low probability to dangerous completions.

Evaluation should center on matched hidden-world families: identical pre-decision observations with, for example, an empty occlusion, a crossing pedestrian, or an emerging vehicle. Metrics are collision rate under adversarial completions, unnecessary stopping in empty completions, time until information permits progress, and violations of the invariant stopping set. This directly tests whether the vehicle handles uncertainty caused by unavailable information, rather than merely producing diverse trajectories that look plausible in an open-loop benchmark.
